course.title: Principles of Marketing
course.description: A practical first course in marketing — what it really is, how the marketing mix works, and how firms find, win, and keep customers. Structure adapted from OpenStax Principles of Marketing (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: Marketing is best defined as…
options: creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers
questions.explanation: Marketing is the whole process of creating and delivering value — selling is only one part. See 'What marketing really is'.

questions.prompt: The 'marketing concept' says a firm should start with…
questions.explanation: The marketing concept is customer-first, not product-first. See 'What marketing really is'.

questions.prompt: The classic '4 Ps' of the marketing mix are Product, Price, Place, and…
questions.explanation: Product, Price, Place, Promotion — covered in 'The marketing mix'.

questions.prompt: Dividing a broad market into smaller groups with shared traits is called…
questions.explanation: Segmentation comes first in STP — see 'Segmentation, targeting, positioning'.

questions.prompt: A shopper comparing three phone brands before buying is in which stage of the buyer decision process?
questions.explanation: Comparing options is the search-and-evaluation stage — see 'Consumer behavior'.

questions.prompt: The extra value a well-known name adds to a product is called brand…
questions.explanation: Brand equity is the value the name itself carries — see the key terms and quizzes.

questions.prompt: A 'position' in positioning refers to…
options: a shelf location in a store
the place a brand holds in the customer's mind versus rivals
a job title in the marketing team
questions.explanation: Positioning is about perception in the customer's mind — see 'Segmentation, targeting, positioning'.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of earned media (not paid or owned)?
options: a TV ad the brand buys
questions.explanation: Earned media is coverage you didn't pay for — see 'Digital and social media marketing'.

lessons.title: What marketing really is
lessons.grammar_note: Marketing ≠ selling. Selling pushes what you made; marketing starts with what the customer needs.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define marketing and explain the marketing concept. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, is 'marketing' the same as 'advertising'? Why not?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Marketing is the process of *creating, communicating, and delivering value* to customers, and doing it profitably. Notice it is far bigger than ads. The guiding philosophy is the *marketing concept*: start with the customer's needs and wants, then build the offer — instead of making a product and hoping someone buys it (the older 'production' or 'selling' orientations). Value is the customer's simple mental math: *benefits minus costs*. A firm wins when its offer gives more value than the alternatives.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Netflix did not begin by asking 'how do we sell DVDs faster?' It asked 'what do renters hate?' — late fees and trips to the store. Streaming answered a customer *need*, not a factory's output. That is the marketing concept in action: needs first, product second.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as production-oriented or marketing-oriented: (1) 'We make 10,000 units a day, now push them out.' (2) 'Customers said checkout is slow, so we redesigned it.' (3) 'Our engineers love this feature, ship it regardless of demand.' (4) 'We surveyed users and built the top-requested tool.' Answers: (1) production, (2) marketing, (3) production, (4) marketing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking marketing just means promotion. Mistake: assuming a great product sells itself without understanding customer value. Exit: (a) In one word, what does the marketing concept put first? (b) Value = benefits minus what? Answers: the customer (needs); costs.

lessons.title: The marketing mix: the 4 Ps
lessons.grammar_note: Product, Price, Place, Promotion — change one P and you often must adjust the others.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the 4 Ps and explain how they work together. Warm-up: which 'P' covers *where* a customer can buy the product?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *marketing mix* is the set of controllable tools a firm uses to reach its target market, summarized as the *4 Ps*: *Product* (the goods, service, or experience and its features), *Price* (what the customer pays and how), *Place* (distribution — how and where it becomes available), and *Promotion* (how the firm communicates value: advertising, sales, social media). The mix must be *internally consistent*: a premium product with a bargain price and a discount-store placement sends mixed signals.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Consider a premium coffee brand like a Starbucks-style chain. *Product*: crafted drinks and a 'third place' atmosphere. *Price*: high, signaling quality. *Place*: prime, high-foot-traffic corners plus a mobile app. *Promotion*: loyalty rewards and seasonal launches, not deep price-cut ads. Every P reinforces 'premium'. Now swap in a dollar-price and a vending-machine Place — the whole story collapses.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Sort each decision into a P: (1) offering a 3-year warranty, (2) selling only through the brand's own app, (3) a buy-one-get-one deal, (4) charging a subscription instead of a one-time fee. Answers: (1) Product, (2) Place, (3) Promotion, (4) Price.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the 4 Ps as separate checklists instead of one coordinated story. Mistake: filing 'Place' under 'store shelves only' — it means the whole distribution path, including online. Exit: (a) Which P is distribution? (b) Which P is how you communicate value? Answers: Place; Promotion.

lessons.title: Segmentation, targeting, and positioning
lessons.grammar_note: STP order is fixed: Segment the market → Target a segment → Position the brand.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Walk through the STP process and write a positioning statement. Warm-up: why can't one product be 'for everyone'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: No brand can serve every buyer well, so marketers use *STP*. *Segmentation* splits a broad market into groups with shared traits — by demographics (age, income), geography, psychographics (values, lifestyle), or behavior (usage, loyalty). *Targeting* chooses which segment(s) to serve based on size, growth, and fit. *Positioning* then plants a clear, distinct idea of the brand in the target's mind, relative to competitors — often captured in a positioning statement: 'For [target], [brand] is the [category] that [key benefit] because [reason].'

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: The car market segments into many groups. Volvo targets safety-conscious families and *positions* on safety: 'For families who prioritize protection, Volvo is the car brand that delivers class-leading safety because of decades of engineering focused on it.' Meanwhile a brand like Tesla targets tech-forward early adopters and positions on innovation. Same market, different segment, different position.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For a new plant-based protein bar, (1) name one segmentation variable you'd use, (2) pick a target segment, (3) draft a one-line positioning statement. Sample answers: (1) behavior/lifestyle — gym-goers; (2) target: fitness-focused young adults; (3) 'For active young adults, PlantFuel is the protein bar that fuels workouts cleanly because it uses only whole-food plant ingredients.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: doing STP out of order — you cannot position before you know who you target. Mistake: choosing a segment too small or too vague to serve profitably. Exit: (a) What is the correct order of STP? (b) Positioning lives in whose mind? Answers: segment, target, position; the customer's.

questions.prompt: The marketing concept says the firm should begin with…
questions.explanation: Customer needs come first.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the 4 Ps?
questions.explanation: The classic four are Product, Price, Place, Promotion.

questions.prompt: 'Place' in the marketing mix refers to…
options: distribution — how the product reaches buyers
questions.explanation: Place = distribution.

questions.prompt: Grouping customers by lifestyle and values is … segmentation.
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation uses values and lifestyle.

questions.prompt: The correct STP sequence is…
questions.explanation: Segment, then target, then position.

questions.prompt: A premium product sold at a rock-bottom price in a discount store violates which principle?
options: internal consistency of the marketing mix
questions.explanation: The 4 Ps must reinforce one another.

lessons.title: Consumer behavior: how people decide
lessons.grammar_note: The buyer decision process: recognize need → search → evaluate → buy → post-purchase.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the buyer decision process and the main influences on it. Warm-up: what happens in a buyer's mind *before* they even search for options?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Consumers move through a *five-stage buyer decision process*: (1) *need recognition* (a gap between actual and desired state), (2) *information search*, (3) *evaluation of alternatives*, (4) *purchase*, and (5) *post-purchase behavior*, where satisfaction or *cognitive dissonance* (buyer's remorse) sets in. Choices are shaped by *cultural*, *social* (family, reference groups), *personal* (age, income), and *psychological* (motivation, perception, attitudes) factors. High-cost, risky buys get extended decision-making; a habitual snack purchase gets almost none.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Buying a laptop: you notice your old one is slow (need recognition), read reviews and compare specs (search), weigh price against battery life (evaluation), buy the model with the best fit (purchase), then feel reassured or regretful when it arrives (post-purchase). Smart marketers reduce post-purchase dissonance with follow-up emails, easy returns, and setup guides — think of the welcome sequence after you buy an Apple device.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match the stage: (1) 'My phone screen just cracked.' (2) 'I'm reading three comparison articles.' (3) 'I hope I made the right choice.' (4) 'I'll take this one.' Answers: (1) need recognition, (2) information search, (3) post-purchase, (4) purchase.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the sale ends the process — post-purchase experience drives loyalty and word of mouth. Mistake: ignoring social influences like reviews and reference groups. Exit: (a) What is buyer's remorse formally called? (b) Which stage comes right before purchase? Answers: cognitive dissonance; evaluation of alternatives.

lessons.title: Digital and social media marketing
lessons.grammar_note: Three media types: Paid (you buy it), Owned (you control it), Earned (others give it to you).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish paid, owned, and earned media and explain why engagement matters. Warm-up: is a viral customer video paid, owned, or earned?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Digital marketing reaches customers through search, social platforms, email, and content. A useful map is *PESO / paid–owned–earned* media: *paid* (ads you buy — search ads, sponsored posts), *owned* (channels you control — your site, app, email list), and *earned* (coverage others create — shares, reviews, press). Social media adds *engagement*: two-way conversation, not one-way broadcast. Success is measured with metrics like *reach*, *engagement rate*, *conversion rate*, and *return on ad spend*, and increasingly through *influencer* partnerships and short-form video.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A small skincare brand runs Instagram ads (paid), posts tutorials on its own TikTok and emails its list (owned), and then a customer's honest 'holy grail' review goes viral (earned). The earned post costs nothing yet often converts best, because people trust peers over ads. The brand amplifies it by resharing — turning earned momentum into owned content.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each: (1) a Google search ad, (2) the brand's email newsletter, (3) a customer's unpaid TikTok review, (4) a paid influencer post disclosed as an ad. Answers: (1) paid, (2) owned, (3) earned, (4) paid.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating social media as a billboard instead of a conversation. Mistake: chasing follower counts (a vanity metric) while ignoring conversion. Exit: (a) Your own website is which media type? (b) A free viral share is which type? Answers: owned; earned.

items.translation: the controllable 4 Ps — Product, Price, Place, Promotion — a firm blends to reach its market
items.example: A consistent marketing mix makes every P tell the same brand story.

items.translation: dividing a broad market into smaller groups that share needs or traits
items.example: Segmentation by lifestyle separated the gym-goers from the casual snackers.

items.translation: the distinct place a brand occupies in the target customer's mind versus rivals
the added value a well-known brand name gives a product beyond its features
items.example: Strong brand equity lets Apple charge a premium.

items.translation: post-purchase doubt or 'buyer's remorse' after a decision
items.example: A reassuring follow-up email reduces cognitive dissonance.

items.translation: exposure a brand gains from others (shares, reviews, press) without paying for it
items.example: The viral customer review was pure earned media.

questions.prompt: The five stages of the buyer decision process end with…
questions.explanation: Post-purchase behavior is the final stage.

questions.prompt: Buyer's remorse is formally known as…
questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is post-purchase doubt.

questions.prompt: A brand's own website and email list are examples of … media.
questions.explanation: Owned media is what the brand controls.

questions.prompt: An unpaid, viral customer review is … media.
questions.explanation: Earned media comes from others at no cost.

questions.prompt: The extra value a strong name adds beyond product features is brand…
questions.explanation: That value is brand equity.

questions.prompt: Which social metric is most often called a 'vanity' figure?
questions.explanation: Follower count alone can mislead if it doesn't convert.

lessons.title: Applied project: build a marketing plan for a product

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a real or invented product and write a one-page marketing plan for it. You won't launch it — you'll plan it rigorously, using the concepts from this course.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Describe the product and the customer need it meets. 2) Apply STP: name one segmentation variable, pick a target segment, and write a one-line positioning statement. 3) Spell out all 4 Ps and show they reinforce one another. 4) Sketch a promotion plan naming at least one paid, one owned, and one earned media tactic. 5) State one metric you'd track to judge success.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The product clearly answers a customer need (marketing concept, not production-first). ✔ STP is in order and the positioning statement names target, category, and benefit. ✔ All four Ps are present and internally consistent. ✔ Your promotion mix uses paid, owned, AND earned media. ✔ You chose a real success metric (e.g. conversion rate), not just a vanity number. Hit all five and you've thought like a marketer.
